h1:
Lampam Lake Seafood
Salted Catfish, Fresh Prawns by the Lake
intro: Lampam Beach sits just about 7 km from Phatthalung town, on the shore of Songkhla Lake — the largest brackish-water lagoon in Thailand. The water here mixes fresh and salt, so you get giant river prawns, sea catfish, catfish, shellfish and crab that are hard to find anywhere else. We've pulled together the lake catch worth trying, plus the lakeside spots where you can actually sit and eat with a cool breeze off the water.

blocks.html: Phatthalung runs the whole length of Songkhla Lake's western shore, and people here have eaten brackish-water fish and the lake's fermented foods for generations. The most famous of all is pla duk ra (salted sun-dried catfish) — sea catfish salted and dried in the sun until it takes on its own distinct smell and flavour. Thale Noi and Khuan Khanun are the oldest places making it, so much so that it's earned a Geographical Indication (GI) registration. Come all the way to Phatthalung and skip the fried salted catfish, and you've genuinely missed something.

blocks.text: Lake dishes you have to try

blocks.html: Songkhla Lake is brackish — that is, halfway between sea and river — so the ingredients are a mix of freshwater and saltwater catch. These are the dishes you'll spot often at the Lampam Beach restaurants, and the ones to order if you've made it all the way here.

items.name: Fried salted catfish (pla duk ra thot)
items.blurb: Sea catfish salted and sun-dried, then fried until fragrant — the meat is salty with a faint sweetness and that signature fermented aroma. Eat it with hot steamed rice, a squeeze of lime, sliced shallots and bird's eye chillies. It's a dish whole Phatthalung households eat together. The real thing comes from Thale Noi and Khuan Khanun.
items.meta: Star side dish · 80–150 THB a plate

items.name: Lampam brackish-water river prawns
items.blurb: Big giant river prawns from the lake during the brackish season — firm, sweet meat with plenty of fat in the head. Lakeside spots do them several ways: grilled, salt-baked, topped with salted-egg sauce or steamed in fresh milk. This is Lampam's headline dish, and plenty of people make the trip just for it.
items.meta: Priced by weight · from 500 THB a kilo

items.name: Sour curry with sea catfish (kaeng som pla kot)
items.blurb: Sea catfish is a brackish-water fish with soft meat and slick skin. Southern sour curry is bold — sharp, sour and hot — and takes a range of vegetables, with a deep orange broth. Slurped hot with rice, it's a perfect match, and just about every lakeside restaurant has it.

items.name: Pickled prawns (kung som / kung wan)
items.blurb: Lake prawns fermented the home-style way by the fishing families around the lagoon — sour and a little salty. They're fried or stir-fried with egg and eaten with rice porridge or steamed rice. It's a preserved food you'll only really find around these parts.

items.name: Salt-baked / grilled river prawns
items.blurb: Big giant river prawns grilled or salt-baked — sweet, bouncy meat dipped in punchy seafood sauce. It's an easy order, and you can see the fresh ingredient right in front of you. Pretty much every Lampam Beach spot does these.

items.name: Crispy turmeric-fried small fish (pla luk bre)
items.blurb: Small lake fish rubbed with turmeric and garlic, then fried crisp whole — bones and all are good to eat — with that southern turmeric aroma. It's a snack that works just as well with rice as it does alongside a drink.

items.name: Steamed seafood curry (ho mok thale)
items.blurb: Fish and seafood mixed with southern curry paste, steamed in banana leaf or a cup — rich with the aroma of the paste, soft-textured and well-rounded. It's the dish that lets people who can't take much heat still eat well and happily.

items.name: Roasted crab curry with cha-phlu leaves
items.blurb: Crab meat from the lake with cha-phlu (wild betel) leaves in a roasted coconut-cream curry — fatty, fragrant and creamy in the southern style, not too hot. It goes down easy with steamed rice, and several Lampam seafood spots do this coconut curry especially well.

items.name: Squid in sweet broth (pla muek tom wan)
items.blurb: Squid simmered in a lightly sweet broth — the meat is tender, not chewy. It's a standout at a few spots like Ban Cham, easy to eat and fine for kids, a good pick to order alongside the bolder dishes.

items.name: Mullet (sour curry / fried)
items.blurb: Lake mullet has firm meat that goes into sour curry or gets fried and topped with fish sauce — naturally sweet, the way brackish-water fish are. It's an inexpensive local fish you can find in season.

blocks.title: How to spot real salted catfish
blocks.html: Good salted catfish is dried just enough — the meat is still soft, not blastingly salty, with a fermented smell that's fragrant rather than overpowering. The famous sources are Thale Noi and Khuan Khanun. If you want to buy some home as a gift, pick a vendor in a local market or a shop that states it's made in Thale Noi, and you'll get the genuine local article.

blocks.text: Lakeside spots where you can actually sit and eat

blocks.html: Lampam Beach has seafood restaurants lined up along the lake shore, most with tables jutting out to catch the breeze and the water view. In the evening you'll see the sun set over the lake. These are the spots Phatthalung locals and real reviews bring up most often.

items.name: Kieng Ta Lay Terrace
items.blurb: A local-fusion spot right on Lampam Beach using fresh ingredients from the lake. It's known for the Lampam brackish-water prawns, done several ways — salt-baked, topped with salted-egg sauce, steamed in fresh milk — with a terrace looking out over the lake.

items.name: Ban Cham
items.blurb: A long-running spot on Khlong Pak Pra in Lampam, with a shady wooden deck reaching out over the canal. The standouts are squid in sweet broth, crispy turmeric-fried small fish, and mullet sour curry. Around 100–250 THB a head. Open daily from about 10.30am. Tel 091 848 8599.

items.name: Kanam Rimlae
items.blurb: A restaurant and café right on Lampam Lake, with lakeside tables and a cool breeze. The menu runs to seafood and a well-balanced steamed seafood curry. Good for an evening visit to catch the sunset.

items.name: Sunee Mueang Trang Lampam
items.blurb: A seafood spot on the Lian Khuean–Ban Lampam road, with grilled big prawns as the standout. Around 250–500 THB a head. You can book a table ahead. Tel 086 295 7542.

items.name: Ban Rim Khlong
items.blurb: A waterside restaurant and café on Lampam Lake, done up vintage-style with friendly prices. On weekends there's a morning market and alms-giving on the Lampam bridge. Good for families.

blocks.title: What time to go
blocks.html: If you want the freshest ingredients without a long wait, go before noon or in the late afternoon. If it's the sunset over the lake you're after, sit down around 5.00–6.30pm. Long holiday weekends get busy, so calling ahead to reserve a lakeside table is the safer bet.

Because it's brackish water, some ingredients are seasonal. The big giant river prawns and certain fish are at their fullest late in the year. People around Songkhla and Phatthalung call them pla sam nam or kung sam nam ("three-water" fish and prawns) because they're in the season when three kinds of water mix — the meat is firmer, sweeter and fattier than usual. If you're here at that time and see them on the menu, order them.

items: Big prawns and fish — at their fullest from late in the year into early the next, with prices rising and falling with the catch.
Salted catfish — available year-round since it's salted and dried, so you can buy it as a gift in any season.
Home-style ferments (pickled prawns, shrimp paste) — around all year, the food-preservation know-how of the fishing families around the lake.

blocks.text: Eating at Lampam without missing a thing

items: Start with fresh prawns — go grilled or salt-baked first, so you get the pure flavour of the ingredient.
Order the fried salted catfish to go with hot steamed rice, and don't forget the shallots and lime.
Get one bold curry, like sour curry with sea catfish, to cut through the grilled stuff.
If there's a group of you, add a coconut curry like the roasted crab curry with cha-phlu leaves, or steamed seafood curry, to round out the flavours.
Leave room in your bag to take salted catfish and pickled prawns home as gifts.

faq.q: Where's the best place to eat Phatthalung salted catfish?
faq.a: Salted catfish is a local staple that most southern restaurants and Lampam Beach spots will fry up on request. The famous genuine article comes from Thale Noi and Khuan Khanun, which hold a GI registration. If you want to take some home as a gift, look in local markets and at shops that state it's made in Thale Noi.

faq.q: How far is Lampam Beach from Phatthalung town?
faq.a: Lampam Beach is about 7 km from Phatthalung town, roughly a 15-minute drive. It's the shore of Songkhla Lake, lined with waterside restaurants and with spots to sit and watch the sunset.

faq.q: What are 'three-water' prawns, and why try them?
faq.a: Three-water prawns are giant river prawns from the lake during the brackish season when several kinds of water mix, which makes the meat firmer, sweeter and fattier than usual. They're Lampam's headline dish, usually done grilled, salt-baked or topped with salted-egg sauce. They're at their fullest from late in the year into early the next.

faq.q: When's the best time to eat at the Lampam lakeside?
faq.a: If you want the freshest ingredients without a wait, go before noon or in the late afternoon. If you're after the atmosphere, go around 5.00–6.30pm to catch the sunset over the lake. On long holiday weekends it's best to call ahead and reserve a lakeside table.

faq.q: Roughly how much is a seafood meal at Lampam per person?
faq.a: Most spots run about 100–250 THB a head. If you order big giant river prawns, which are priced by weight, the per-person budget can climb to around 250–500 THB, depending on how much prawn you order.
